slides.title: A cost-seg estimate means something only after your CPA confirms every input
slides.subtitle: Resource SR.3. Cost segregation & tax-impact estimator
meta: Education only. Not tax advice. Your CPA decides every input and result.
slides.notes:
This deck teaches you how to use one tool: the cost segregation and tax-impact estimator. It's a scenario workbook for one property.

It estimates how much depreciation a cost-segregation study might move into year one, and what that could mean for your tax. I built it for the conversation with your CPA. It doesn't replace that conversation.

We'll walk through the whole thing. What it's for, each tab, each section of inputs, the formulas, the rules built into it, and a filled example using Cedar Ridge. Then the common mistakes, the evidence to ask a study provider for, and how to hand it to your CPA.

One warning up front. Whether any of this applies depends on the property, the dates, and how you use it. It also depends on your participation, your income, and the tax year. The workbook makes those inputs visible. Your CPA decides them.

slides.title: The workbook does four jobs, and none of them is deciding your tax
slides.text: Use it after Sam's PA.5 lesson, when you have a real property and a real quote from a study provider.
items: Collects every input a CPA will ask for, with a source and a status beside each.
Separates ordinary depreciation from accelerated depreciation, so you see what the study changes.
Shows the tax effect only after the loss limits you enter, so an unusable deduction never looks like cash.
Lists every assumption still unverified, so nothing gets treated as settled by accident.
slides.notes:
The workbook does four jobs.

First, it collects every input a CPA will ask for, with a source and a status beside each one. Second, it separates ordinary depreciation from accelerated depreciation. That way you can see what the study actually changes, compared with doing nothing.

Third, and this is the one people skip, it shows the tax effect only after the loss limits you enter. A big deduction you can't use this year is not cash this year. The workbook won't let it look like cash.

Fourth, it lists every assumption that's still unverified.

Sam's PA.5 lesson explains what a cost-segregation study is and walks through a year-one example. Watch that first. Bring back the idea of reclassifying parts of the building into shorter lives. Then use this workbook when you have a real address and a real quote from a study provider.

slides.title: Five tabs keep inputs, formulas, and results apart, and only inputs take typing
rows: Every assumption, with what to enter, source, status, and date checked
The separated results you bring to the CPA
Low, base, and high side by side
Every rule the workbook relies on, with link and date

box.label: Status values, used everywhere
box.text: **Verified** (document in hand). **CPA to supply.** **Unverified** (estimate or placeholder). **Study** (from the cost-segregation report).

slides.notes:
Build it as a spreadsheet with five tabs. The formulas later in this deck use these tab names and cell addresses, so keep them exactly.

Inputs holds every assumption. Calc holds formulas only, and nobody types there. Outputs holds the separated results you bring to your CPA. Scenarios puts low, base, and high cases side by side. And Sources lists every rule the workbook relies on, with a link and a date.

Shade the input cells. Those are the only cells anyone types into.

If you'd like, add a sixth tab called Open items to track unresolved questions separately. Otherwise the Outputs tab pulls them from the status column on Inputs.

That status column uses four values everywhere. Verified means you have the document in hand. CPA to supply means it's their call. Unverified means it's an estimate or a placeholder. Study means it comes from the cost-segregation report. In the Cedar Ridge example you'll also see Example input. That marks a teaching figure a real owner would pull from reports and mark Verified.

slides.title: Section 1 records dates and basis, and the contract date matters as much as closing
slides.caption: B3 to B5 hold the address, the owners and entity (PA.10), and the tax year. B12 names the land method.
slides.notes:
The Inputs tab has five sections. Column A is the field, column B is the value, and the next columns hold what to enter, the source, the status, and the date checked. The values here are the Cedar Ridge base case from example B6. All of them are assumptions for teaching.

Section 1 is property and dates. Notice there are three dates, not one. The binding contract date, the closing date, and the placed-in-service date. The contract date matters because property isn't treated as acquired after the date a binding written contract was signed. That's why the workbook asks for it.

Placed in service means the date the property was ready and available for rent. Your listing's live date and first available night help. Your CPA confirms it.

Then the money: purchase price, capitalized closing costs, the land share, improvements before first rental, furnishings, and the study fee. The land share is Unverified until your CPA picks a method, like the assessor ratio, an appraisal, or the study.

slides.title: Sections 2 and 3 take the study's split and screen the bonus rate by date
slides.caption: B17 + B18 + B19 = 22%, the canonical reclass share in B6. Once you have the report, replace them with the study's dollars divided by building basis.
slides.notes:
Section 2 holds the study results. B17, B18, and B19 are the shares of the building the study moves into 5-year, 7-year, and 15-year property. For Cedar Ridge they're 15%, 0%, and 7%. Those add to 22%, the reclass share in our B6 example. The 15-year bucket is often land improvements.

These are placeholders until you have a report. Then you replace them with the study's dollar figures divided by the building basis.

B20 is the recovery period for the rest of the building, 27.5 or 39 years. That's your CPA's call, and we'll see why in the rules.

Section 3 is bonus depreciation. B21 is a formula, not a typed number. It checks whether the contract, closing, and placed-in-service dates all fall after January 19, 2025. If they do, it shows 100%. If not, it shows the word CPA. B22 stays blank unless your CPA enters a different rate or an election.

slides.title: Sections 4 and 5 capture use, hours, and loss limits, the inputs that decide usability
rows: Days rented at a fair rental price
Number of stays / days in all rental periods
Participation test relied on / real estate professional
Share of year-1 loss usable this year
slides.notes:
Section 4 is use, participation, and loss limits. These are the inputs that decide whether a deduction becomes cash this year.

Days rented, stays, and days in all rental periods come from your platform and PMS reports. For Cedar Ridge I've used 212 days and 61 stays. Those are example inputs, an assumption, so the status says so. With a real property, you'd pull them from your reports and mark them Verified. Personal-use days come from your calendar, and your CPA applies the definition. Maya and Chris plan about 10.

B27 and B28 ask for your hours and everyone else's. The cleaner, the co-host, the manager. Keep a contemporaneous log. It's Unverified until someone reviews it.

Then the CPA cells: which participation test applies, professional status, MAGI, the usable share, and the rates. In the base case the usable share is 100% and the state rate is a 0% placeholder.

Section 5 has two switches. B35 picks a full first year, which matches B6, or the mid-month fraction. B36 turns on dividing expenses by rental days. The canonical case uses neither.

slides.title: The Calc tab keeps land out of every depreciation line below cell B5
slides.caption: B14 and B15 cover any bonus rate under 100% (the CPA's software computes B15). B17 is the first-year fraction; B18 applies it; B20 is the rental-use fraction.
slides.notes:
The Calc tab is formulas only. Each row is one cell in column B.

Start with basis: purchase price plus capitalized costs plus early improvements. That's $391,000 for Cedar Ridge. B4 and B5 are the heart of the land rule. Land sits outside every depreciation line. No formula below B5 touches B4.

The building is $312,800. The study's shares move $68,816 of it into short lives, leaving $243,984. Add the furnishings and you get $100,816 of bonus-eligible basis.

Look at B12. If your CPA entered an override, it uses that. If the date screen returned a number, it uses that. If the screen returned CPA, it falls back to zero. That's on purpose. A failed date screen shows no bonus until your CPA enters a rate.

The remaining building runs straight-line at $6,256 a year over 39 years. Year one in the base case is $107,072. B14 and B15 only matter when bonus is under 100%. Don't estimate those by hand.

slides.title: The lower Calc rows apply the flags, the usable share, and the no-study comparison
rows: Shows the Pub 925 message when the average stay is 7 days or less
Tests personal days against the greater of 14 or 10% of rented days
Furnishings bonus + building at B20 years
slides.caption: B31 is the added tax effect from the study ($21,456). B33 and B34 carry the accelerated ($100,816) and straight-line ($6,256) pools to the Outputs tab.
slides.notes:
The lower half of the Calc tab turns a deduction into something you can reason about.

B22 divides days in all rental periods by the number of stays. For Cedar Ridge that's 3.48 days. B23 flags an average stay of 7 days or less, which sends your CPA to a specific Publication 925 test. B24 runs the home-use day test.

Then the money. B25 multiplies the deduction by the usable share your CPA enters. Whatever isn't usable lands in B26 as carried forward or suspended. B27 applies the rates. That's $34,263 in the base case, only if every input holds.

B29 is the comparison I care most about: year one with no study at all. Furniture still gets bonus, and the whole building runs straight-line. That's $40,021. So B30, the study's added deduction, is $67,051.

B32 is adjusted basis after year one, $315,928. That's the starting point for any future gain.

slides.title: The Outputs tab keeps ordinary, accelerated, and usable amounts on separate lines
rows: Bonus on reclassified parts and furnishings
Not lost, but not cash this year
Starting point for any future gain

box.label: Top line of the tab, in bold
box.text: Illustrative only. Every figure depends on inputs your CPA has not yet confirmed. Not tax advice.

slides.notes:
The Outputs tab is what you bring to the CPA. Keep these lines separate. Never add them together into one big number.

Ordinary depreciation is $6,256. Accelerated is $100,816. Together that's a $107,072 estimated deduction, before loss limits. Then usable this year, and carried forward. In the base case all of it is usable, but that's an assumption your CPA has to confirm.

The tax effect is labeled illustrative for a reason. It's $34,263 only if every input holds.

The two pools at the bottom matter later. The accelerated pool is mostly section 1245 items, which means ordinary-income recapture exposure at sale, up to the gain on those assets. Your CPA classifies the 15-year land improvements. The straight-line pool is unrecaptured section 1250 exposure, taxed at a maximum 25%. OP.12 picks both up.

Put the disclaimer line at the top of the tab in bold. And the tab also lists the flags and every input that isn't Verified.

slides.title: Six mistakes turn an honest estimate into a number that looks like cash
items: Adding the tax effect to operating cash flow or to a lender's math. Keep it on its own line.
Treating the estimated deduction as cash before the CPA sets the usable share.
Typing into the Calc tab. Only the shaded input cells take typing.
Guessing a CPA cell instead of leaving it blank and marking its status.
Applying bonus to land or to the whole building. Land never depreciates.
Counting furniture twice: once in B14 and again inside the study.
slides.notes:
Here are the mistakes this workbook is built to catch.

The biggest is mixing the tax effect into cash flow. Never add it to operating cash flow in another model. And keep it out of lender math. A lender underwrites cash flow, not deductions.

Second, treating the deduction as cash before your CPA sets the usable share. If the activity is passive, that share can be zero.

Third, typing into the Calc tab. Once someone overwrites a formula, nobody can trust the outputs.

Fourth, guessing. If a cell is your CPA's call, leave it blank and mark it CPA to supply. A guess dressed up as a number is worse than an empty cell.

Fifth, bonus on land or on the whole building. Bonus applies to the short-life pieces only.

Sixth, counting furniture twice. If your furnishings are already on your books in B14, ask the study provider how they treated them.

slides.title: Five built-in rules decide whether the deduction can count this year

gates.q: Were the contract, closing, and placed-in-service dates all after Jan. 19, 2025?
gates.no: Shows CPA; bonus is 0 until entered

gates.q: Is the asset short-life property, 20 years or less?
gates.sub: Reclassified parts plus furnishings: $100,816. The 39-year building is not.

gates.q: Is personal use at or under the greater of 14 days or 10% of rented days?
gates.no: Used as a home: Pub 527 limits

gates.q: Is the average stay 7 days or less?
After participation tests and loss limits, is the loss usable?

slides.end: All five clear: tax effect = usable deduction × your CPA's rates. Still illustrative.
slides.notes:
The workbook builds in eight rules. Five of them work like gates.

Gate one is dates. The IRS says 100% bonus is now permanent for eligible property acquired after January 19, 2025. A binding contract signed earlier changes that, which is why B6 exists. Publication 946 also describes 40% for certain earlier property, and an election to take 40% instead. The screen only checks dates. Your CPA confirms eligibility.

Gate two: bonus needs a recovery period of 20 years or less. The building's 27.5 or 39 years is too long. Land isn't depreciable at all.

Gate three is the Publication 527 home-use test. Cedar Ridge's 10 personal days sit under 21.2.

Gate four is Publication 925's average-stay rule. Cedar Ridge averages 3.48 days. Passing that doesn't make the loss usable by itself. It sends your CPA to the material participation tests, like more than 500 hours, or more than 100 hours and at least as much as anyone else. A cleaner who logs more hours than you can matter here.

slides.title: Four more rules keep the building life, loss limits, and basis honest
items: Building life is a CPA call. At 27.5 years, Cedar Ridge's remaining building is $8,872 a year instead of $6,256.
The $25,000 allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of MAGI. At about $185,000 it's gone either way.
The excess business loss limit was $313,000, or $626,000 joint, for 2025. Your CPA supplies the current year.
A study on property placed in service in an earlier year can need Form 3115 and a section 481(a) adjustment.
Depreciation reduces basis whether or not you claim it. The Outputs tab carries both pools to OP.12.
slides.notes:
Here are the other rules.

The building life. Publication 946 defines residential rental property by where the income comes from, and it excludes hotel, motel, or inn units used mostly on a transient basis. How that applies to a single house rented for short stays is a question for your CPA. B6 uses 39 years. At 27.5, Cedar Ridge's line would be $8,872 a year.

Loss limits come before the tax effect. Publication 925 describes a special allowance of up to $25,000 for active participation. It phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of MAGI. Ask whether it can apply at all. At Maya and Chris's assumed $185,000, it's fully phased out anyway. There's also an excess business loss limit. For 2025 it was $313,000, or $626,000 joint.

A late study can need Form 3115. Your CPA handles that filing.

And depreciation reduces basis whether or not you claim it. That's why the pools carry forward.

slides.title: Worked by hand, Cedar Ridge's base case gives a $107,072 year-1 deduction
slides.side:
Remaining building: $312,800 - $68,816 = $243,984.

At 32%, the illustrative tax effect is **$34,263**, only if all of it is usable this year.
slides.notes:
Here's the base column worked by hand, so you can follow each formula.

Basis is $385,000 plus $6,000 of capitalized costs, or $391,000. Land at 20% is $78,200. The building is $312,800.

The study reclassifies 22% of the building, which is $68,816. That leaves $243,984 of remaining building.

Accelerated depreciation is the reclassified parts plus the $32,000 of furnishings, at 100% bonus. That's $100,816, if eligible.

Ordinary depreciation is $243,984 divided by 39, or $6,256.

Add them and the year-one deduction is $107,072.

At an assumed 32% marginal rate, the illustrative tax effect is $34,263. I keep saying illustrative because that number only holds if every input holds, and if all of the deduction is usable this year. Every figure on this slide is an assumption from example B6.

slides.title: Land and reclass shares alone swing the year-1 deduction from $79,020 to $137,670
rows: Illustrative tax effect at 32%, if usable
slides.caption: Only two inputs change. Low and high land on the same remaining building by coincidence, not by rule.
slides.notes:
This is the Scenarios tab. The low and high columns change only two inputs: the land share and the reclassified share of the building. Everything else stays at the base values.

In the low case, land is 30% and the study moves 15% of the building. The year-one deduction is $79,020. In the high case, land is 15% and the study moves 30%. The deduction is $137,670.

That's a wide range from two inputs. It tells you where to spend your questions. Ask your CPA how the land share will be set, and ask the study provider how they support the reclass share.

Notice the last row. The bigger the year-one deduction, the lower your adjusted basis. In the high case, basis drops to $285,330. That feeds straight into the gain at sale in OP.12.

And a small note: low and high happen to land on the same remaining-building figure, $232,645. That's a coincidence of these two inputs.

slides.title: The passive case is the one to fear: the full deduction and $0 of tax effect this year
slides.text: Illustrative tax effect at 32%. Each row changes one thing from the base case.

items.label: Mid-month, placed in service in June
Passive, no loss usable this year

slides.caption: The study adds $67,051 of year-1 deduction over no study: $21,456 at 32%, or $16,956 after the $4,500 fee, if fully usable. In the passive case, $107,072 carries forward.
slides.notes:
Now the adjustments your CPA is likely to raise. Each bar changes one thing from the base case.

Mid-month convention, placed in service in June: the building gets 6.5 months, $3,389 instead of $6,256. The tax effect drops to $33,346. Dividing expenses by rental use, 212 out of 222 days, drops it to $32,720.

No study at all: furniture still gets bonus, because it's short-life property either way. The building runs at 39 years. That's $12,807.

And the passive case. If the activity is passive and no loss is usable this year, the tax effect this year is zero. The deduction isn't lost. It waits.

So the study's real contribution, compared with no study, is $67,051 more deduction in year one. At 32% that's $21,456, or $16,956 after the fee, if fully usable. Decide on the study only after you see that line, the passive case, and the fee side by side.

slides.title: Ask a study provider for twelve pieces of evidence before you pay
slides.text: IRS Pub 5653 says there are no standards for preparing studies. The first five requests come from it; the rest make the study usable here.
items: Preparer's name, credentials, and experience
Every participant and their role
Name and description of the method
Reconciliation to price and basis
Source of plans, or site-visit notes and photos
Asset-by-asset schedule with class and life
Legal reasoning for each classification
Land allocation method and support
How furnishings already on your books were treated
Placed-in-service date the study assumed
Discussion of recapture at sale
Fee, delivery date, and support if the IRS asks
slides.notes:
The IRS publishes a Cost Segregation Audit Techniques Guide for its own examiners. It's Publication 5653, and the current version is dated February 2025.

It says there are no standards for preparing these studies. It says they vary widely in method, documentation, depth, and preparer expertise. It describes approaches from a detailed engineering approach built on actual cost records, down to survey, letter, and rule-of-thumb approaches.

Its principal elements of a quality study include a preparer with expertise and experience, and a reconciliation of allocated costs to actual costs. Its information requests ask who prepared the study, what role each person played, and where the blueprints came from.

So use that guide to shape what you ask for before you pay. The first five requests on this list come straight from it. The rest are my recommendations for making the study fit this workbook. The asset schedule fills B17 to B19. The land method ties to B11. The placed-in-service date must match B8.

slides.title: Hand the workbook to your CPA in six steps, dates and basis first
items: Before the meeting, fill every input you can document. Leave CPA cells blank and mark status honestly.
Send the workbook, settlement statement, receipts, study quote, and day calendar.
Ask for dates and basis first (B8, B10, B11, B20), then method choices (B21, B22, B35, B36).
Ask for participation, limits, and rates (B29 to B34). Bring your hour log.
Rerun the Scenarios tab with the CPA's inputs. Save a dated copy and log the CPA on the Sources tab.
Decide on the study after seeing the added deduction, the passive case, and the fee side by side.

box.label: A script for the meeting
box.text: Here is my estimate and every assumption behind it. Which inputs are wrong, which apply to me, and what would you enter instead?

slides.notes:
Here's how to use this with a CPA.

Before the meeting, fill in every input you can document. Leave the CPA cells blank rather than guessing. Mark each status honestly.

Send the workbook with the settlement statement, the furnishing receipts, the study quote, and your calendar of rental and personal days. If you already have the study, send it with the evidence list.

In the meeting, go in order. Dates and basis first: placed in service, capitalized costs, land method, building life. Then method choices: the bonus rate or election, the rental-use division, and the first-year convention. Then participation and limits. Bring your hour log. Then the marginal federal and state rates.

Afterward, rerun the Scenarios tab with their inputs. Save a dated copy and note the CPA's name and date on the Sources tab. Keep that copy with your tax records for OP.12.

And if you're not sure how to open the conversation, read them the script on this slide.

slides.title: Log every rule on the Sources tab, and add a row each time your CPA confirms one
rows: 100% bonus after Jan. 19, 2025; binding contract rule; 40% election
20-year limit for bonus; land; mid-month; transient-use exclusion
Personal-use day test; expense division; allowable depreciation
slides.caption: All rows checked 2026-09-25. The full tab adds Date checked and Checked by columns, plus rows for Form 461, Form 3115, Pub 544, and Topic 409.
slides.notes:
The Sources tab has one row per rule. For each, write the claim, the source with a link, how it was checked, the date, and who checked it.

Here's how we filled it for the rules in this workbook. The bonus rate and binding contract rule trace to an IRS news release and Notice 2026-11. The 20-year limit, the land rule, the mid-month convention, and the transient-use exclusion trace to Publication 946. The day test and allowable depreciation trace to Publication 527. The 7-day rule and participation tests trace to Publication 925. The study quality elements trace to Publication 5653.

We checked these through search summaries of irs.gov on the date shown. That's not the same as your CPA confirming them for your return.

So the most important row is the last one. Each time your CPA confirms an input, add a row with their name, the date, and where they said it. An email counts. That row is the record behind every input your CPA confirms.

box.label: The row that matters most
box.text: Add a row each time your CPA confirms an input, with their name and the date. An email counts.

slides.title: For Cedar Ridge, eleven groups of inputs are still open, and Outputs lists every one
items: Contract, closing, and placed-in-service dates (B6 to B8)
Capitalized acquisition costs of $6,000 (B10)
Land share of 20% and its method (B11, B12)
Study fee and the 15% / 0% / 7% split (B15, B17 to B19)
Building life, 39 vs 27.5 years (B20)
Bonus eligibility and any election (B21, B22)
Rental days and stays, example inputs (B23, B25, B26)
Personal days and expense division (B24, B36)
Owner and others' hours; the participation test (B27 to B29)
MAGI, usable share, and tax rates (B31 to B34)
First-year convention (B35)
slides.notes:
This is the open list. The Outputs tab filters the Inputs tab for every status that isn't Verified. For the Cedar Ridge teaching example, it comes out to these eleven groups.

Look at how much is on it. The dates that drive the bonus rate. The capitalized costs. The land share and method. The study fee and the reclass split. The building life. Bonus eligibility. The rental days and stays, which are example inputs until real reports replace them. Personal days and whether expenses are divided. Hours and the participation test. MAGI, the usable share, and the rates. And the first-year convention.

That's almost every input that moves the answer. So the $34,263 on the Outputs tab sits on top of all eleven open questions.

That's the honest state of any estimate before the CPA meeting. The goal of the meeting is to shrink this list. Each item your CPA confirms comes off, and the estimate gets more real.

slides.title: Your CPA confirms nearly every input, and the study provider confirms its own work
rows: Placed-in-service date, basis, land method, building recovery period, bonus eligibility and election, first-year convention, personal-use division
Whether the activity is passive, which participation test applies, the usable share this year, and which loss limits apply
Marginal federal and state rates; whether Form 3115 is needed for property placed in service in an earlier year
Method, preparer qualifications, participant roles, reconciliation, asset schedule, and fee, before you engage
How the Outputs tab's depreciation pools are treated at a sale or exchange (OP.12)
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what.

Your CPA confirms the dates and basis: placed-in-service date, basis, land method, and building recovery period. Also bonus eligibility, any election, the first-year convention, and whether expenses are divided for personal use.

Your CPA also confirms the loss side. Is the activity passive? Which material participation test applies? How much of the loss is usable this year, and which limits apply?

Then the rates, and whether you need Form 3115 because the study covers property placed in service in an earlier year.

The study provider confirms their own work, in writing, before you engage them. Method, qualifications, who did what, the reconciliation, the asset schedule, and the fee.

And later, at a sale or exchange, your CPA tells you how the depreciation pools on the Outputs tab will be treated. That's the OP.12 conversation.

slides.title: Four steps this week get the workbook ready for your CPA meeting
items: Build the five tabs and enter the Section 1 inputs you can document today.

slides.title: Every rule in the workbook traces to an IRS publication, notice, or form

items.title: IRS: guidance on the additional first-year depreciation deduction (One, Big, Beautiful Bill)
IRS Notice 2026-11
items.note: Interim guidance; binding written contract rule

items.title: IRS Publication 946
items.note: 20-year limit for bonus; land; rates by date; transient exclusion; mid-month

items.title: IRS Publication 527
items.note: Personal-use day test; expense division; allowable depreciation

items.title: IRS Publication 925
items.note: 7-day rule; participation tests; $25,000 allowance and phase-out

items.title: IRS: About Form 3115
items.note: Change in accounting method for late studies

items.title: IRS Publication 5653, Cost Segregation Audit Techniques Guide
items.note: No standards; methods; quality elements; information requests

slides.notes:
These are the sources the workbook relies on.

The IRS news release and Notice 2026-11 cover the permanent 100% bonus for property acquired after January 19, 2025, the binding contract rule, and the 40% election. Publication 946 covers the 20-year limit, the land rule, the rates by date, the residential rental definition, and the mid-month convention.

Publication 527 covers the personal-use day test and allowable depreciation. Publication 925 covers the 7-day rule, the participation tests, and the $25,000 allowance. The Form 461 instructions give the 2025 excess business loss thresholds. Form 3115 covers late studies. Publication 5653 is the examiners' guide to cost-segregation studies. Publication 544 and Topic 409 cover what happens at sale.

The Cedar Ridge figures come from example B6. The low and high cases, the study fee, the reclass split, and the adjustments are new assumptions for teaching. Tax rules change by year, so check each one with your CPA.
